pages.title: David and Goliath
pages.summary: Israel's army and the Philistines face each other across a valley, and for forty days a giant named Goliath dares anyone to fight him. King Saul and his soldiers are terrified. David, the youngest son of Jesse, arrives with food for his brothers and cannot believe that nobody will answer the challenge. He reminds Saul that he has already protected his father's sheep from a lion and a bear. He tries on the king's armour but takes it off, and goes out with a staff, a sling and five smooth stones from the stream. He tells Goliath that the battle belongs to the LORD. One stone brings the giant down, and the Philistines run. The men of Israel and Judah chase them and win the battle for King Saul and for all Israel.
pages.look_closer: Notice what David says he is trusting. It is not his sling. It is the LORD who rescued him from the lion and the bear, and who he says will rescue Israel now (verses 37 and 45-47).
lessons: David knows that the God he serves is bigger than any giant. He trusts the LORD who rescued him from the lion and the bear (1 Samuel 17:37), and he says the battle belongs to the LORD (17:47).
David wins the war for Saul. When a whole army was afraid, one shepherd who trusted God turned the day for all Israel (17:50-52).
Our own giants are met the same way: David refuses the king's armour and goes out in the name of the LORD (17:38-45).

passages.label: David and Goliath face to face

pages.title: Jesus Calms the Storm
pages.summary: After a long day of teaching the crowds beside the lake, Jesus tells his followers to cross to the other side. Several of them are fishermen who know these waters. Jesus falls asleep on a cushion at the back of the boat, and then a fierce windstorm blows up and the waves break over the sides. The disciples wake him, frightened, and ask whether he cares that they are about to drown. Jesus speaks sharply to the wind and tells the sea to be still, and everything goes completely calm. He asks them why they are afraid and where their faith has gone. They are filled with awe and ask one another who he can be, if the wind and the sea listen to him.
pages.look_closer: Notice what happens to their fear. They were afraid of the storm; afterwards they are filled with awe, a deep reverence for Jesus (verse 41), because now they have seen who is in the boat.
lessons: Their fear of the storm gives way to reverence once they see who Jesus is: wind and sea alike obey him (Mark 4:41).
Jesus is in the boat with them, even while he sleeps. He asks them to trust him instead of fearing (4:40).

pages.title: The Prodigal Son
pages.summary:
Jesus tells three stories about something lost and found: a sheep (Luke 15:3-7), a coin (15:8-10) and a son (15:11-32). Each ends with the same joy over the one who is found.

In the third, a younger son asks for his share of the property, leaves for a distant country and spends it all. A famine comes, and he ends up feeding pigs. At last he decides to go home and ask to be treated as a hired worker. While he is still far away, his father sees him, runs to meet him and welcomes him with a robe, a ring and a feast. The older brother, who stayed and worked, is angry. His father goes out to him too, and says that it is right to celebrate when a brother who was lost is found.
pages.look_closer: Notice that the story has two lost sons: one who left and one who stays outside the party. Jesus does not say whether the older brother went in.
lessons: The same lesson three times: heaven rejoices over one lost person who is found (Luke 15:7, 10, 32).
God is like the father who runs to meet his child while he is still far away (15:20): ready to forgive and to welcome home.
Do not stay outside the party. The older brother is invited in too (15:28-32).

context.label: Why Jesus told it: the lost sheep and the lost coin

pages.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
pages.summary: Daniel is one of the three administrators of the Persian king Darius, and he does his work so well that the king plans to put him over the whole kingdom. The other officials are jealous, and since they can find no fault in Daniel they trick the king into signing a law: for thirty days anyone who prays to any god or person except the king will be thrown to the lions. Daniel goes home, opens his window toward Jerusalem and prays three times a day, as he always has. The officials report him, and the king, grieved, cannot undo the law. Daniel is put in the lions' den. At first light the king hurries there, and Daniel answers: God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths. Daniel is lifted out unharmed, and Darius sends out a decree honouring the living God.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Daniel changes nothing. He prays the same way, at the same times, as he did before the law was made, even though he knows what it will cost.
lessons: Keep praying, whatever it costs. Daniel prays three times a day as he always did, though it is now against the law (Daniel 6:10).
A life of integrity is noticed: his enemies could find nothing wrong in him (6:4). Be the same in public and in private.
God shuts the mouths of lions: his angel kept Daniel safe because he trusted his God (6:22-23; Hebrews 11:33).
A faithful life points others to God: King Darius tells the whole kingdom to honour the living God (6:25-27).

passages.label: Daniel prays and is thrown to the lions

pages.title: The Creation
pages.summary: At the start the earth is dark, empty and covered with deep water, with God's Spirit hovering over it. Then God speaks, and there is light. Over six days, each closing with evening and morning, he shapes the world: a sky, then dry land and seas, then plants and fruit trees. He puts lights in the sky, and the stars, to govern day and night and to mark the seasons. He fills the water with sea creatures and the sky with birds, and blesses them, and then he makes the animals of the land. Last, God makes human beings, male and female, in his own image, and puts them in charge of the other living things. Again and again he sees that what he has made is good, and at the end he calls it very good. On the seventh day he rests, blesses it and sets it apart as holy.
pages.look_closer: Notice the steady pattern: God speaks, it happens, he looks at it and calls it good. The wording changes only once, after people are made, when he calls everything very good (verse 31).
lessons: God made everything by his word and called it good (Genesis 1:3-4, 31). The world is no accident: a good God made it on purpose.
People are made in God's image, male and female, and given care of the earth (1:26-28). Every person has worth because of who made them.
God rested on the seventh day and made it holy (2:2-3). Jesus says the day of rest was made for people (Mark 2:27): rest is a gift.
The Bible says all things were made through Jesus and for him (John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:16).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on how to read the six days of Genesis 1: some take them as ordinary days, some as long ages, and some as a way of presenting God's work, and they also differ on how the chapter relates to the age of the earth and to science. This page says only what the text says and takes no side.

pages.title: Noah and the Flood
pages.summary: Violence fills the world, but Noah, a righteous man, walks with God. God tells him a flood is coming and gives him plans for a huge boat, the ark. Noah does everything as he is told. He, his wife, his three sons and their wives go aboard with animals and birds of every kind, and the LORD himself shuts Noah in. Rain falls for forty days and the water stays high for 150, covering even the mountains; every living thing on dry land dies except those in the ark. Then God remembers Noah, sends a wind, and the water slowly drops. The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, but Noah must keep waiting. He sends out a raven, then a dove three times, until the dove stays away. Even when the ground looks dry, he stays inside until God says to come out: about a year in all. Then Noah builds an altar, and God sets his rainbow in the clouds as the sign of his promise.
pages.look_closer: Notice the careful dates. Noah enters the ark on the 17th day of the second month of his 600th year (7:11). God tells him to leave after the 27th day of the second month of the next year (8:14-16): a little over a year. The ark rested in the seventh month (8:4), and months of waiting followed.
lessons: The LORD himself shut Noah in (Genesis 7:16). The God who told Noah to build the ark also guarded him inside it: a picture of God's personal protection over those who obey him.

After the rain stopped, Noah still waited many months, sending out birds again and again, and he left the ark only when God said so. It teaches patience: to wait on God, for his right time, and not to rush things.

passages.label: God tells Noah to build the ark

pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on how to understand the flood: whether it covered the whole earth or a large region, and how the account relates to what scientists find. This page says only what the text says and takes no side.

pages.title: Moses in the Basket
pages.summary: Pharaoh has ordered that every Hebrew baby boy be killed, though the girls may live (Exodus 1:16, 22). A woman of the house of Levi has a son, and seeing how beautiful he is, she hides him for three months. Soon she cannot hide him, so she makes a papyrus basket, coats the basket with tar and pitch, and sets the baby in it among the reeds beside the river. His sister stands nearby to watch. Pharaoh's daughter comes down to bathe, sees the basket and sends a servant to bring it. She finds the baby crying and feels sorry for him, knowing he is a Hebrew child. His sister offers to fetch a Hebrew woman to nurse him. Pharaoh's daughter agrees, and the girl brings the baby's own mother, who is paid to nurse him. When the boy is older he becomes the daughter's son, and she names him Moses, because she pulled him from the water.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Pharaoh's daughter knows at once that this is a Hebrew child (verse 6), the very kind of baby her father has ordered killed (Exodus 1:22), and she still takes pity on him.
lessons: God protects his plan. A king's cruel order could not stop God's rescuer: Moses' parents hid him by faith and were not afraid of the king's command (Exodus 2:2-3; Hebrews 11:23).
God uses ordinary people and small acts: the midwives who feared God (1:17), a mother, a sister, even Pharaoh's daughter (2:5-9).
God put Moses in the palace of the very king who wanted him dead, and prepared him there to free his people (2:10; Acts 7:21-22). He can turn danger into preparation.
God watches over us even when we cannot see how. Moses' sister waited a little way off to see what would be done (2:4).

context.label: Why the baby was hidden: Pharaoh's order

pages.title: Crossing the Red Sea
pages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to camp beside the sea. Pharaoh changes his mind about letting the people go, and chases after them with six hundred of his finest chariots, plus every other chariot in Egypt. The Israelites are terrified. They call out to the LORD for help and blame Moses for bringing them out to die. Moses tells them not to be afraid, because the LORD himself will do the fighting. At the LORD's word Moses holds his hand out over the sea. The angel of God and the pillar of cloud move behind Israel, between the two camps, and all night a strong east wind drives the sea back. The Israelites walk across on dry ground, a wall of water on each side. When the Egyptians follow, the LORD throws their army into confusion, and at daybreak the water rushes back over them all. Israel sees the dead Egyptians on the shore and trusts the LORD and Moses his servant.
pages.look_closer: Notice what happens to the pillar of cloud and the angel of God. They had been going in front of Israel, but now they move behind and stand between the two camps all night (verses 19-20).
lessons: Do not be afraid. Stand firm and watch what the LORD will do; he will fight for you (Exodus 14:13-14).
God makes a way where there is no way: the sea became dry ground (14:21-22). Our impossible is not impossible to him.
God goes before and behind us: the pillar of cloud moved between his people and the enemy all night (14:19-20).
Remember what God has done. After the rescue the people trusted the LORD and his servant Moses (14:31) and sang to him (15:1).

pages.title: The Fall of Jericho
pages.summary: Jericho is shut up tight against Israel. The LORD tells Joshua that he has already handed the city over, and gives a plan that is nothing like a normal attack. For six days the armed men march once around the city, with seven priests blowing ram's horns ahead of the ark of the covenant, while the people stay silent. Each time they go back to camp. On the seventh day they march around seven times, and Joshua tells the people to shout. He says that the city is a gift from the LORD, that everything in it is devoted to the LORD and is to be destroyed, and that only Rahab and her household will be spared, since she hid the spies. The people shout and the wall collapses, and they take the city. The spies bring Rahab and her family out to safety, and Israel burns the city, keeping its silver, gold, bronze and iron for the LORD's treasury.
pages.look_closer: Notice that the two spies keep the promise they made to Rahab in chapter 2. Joshua sends them to bring her and her family out (verses 22-23), and the text adds that she has made her home among the Israelites ever since (verse 25).
lessons: Obey God even when the plan looks strange: a march and silence, not weapons (Joshua 6:3-5). God's ways are higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8-9).
Faith and obedience go together: the walls fell after the people had done what God said for seven days (Joshua 6:15-20; Hebrews 11:30).
God keeps faith with those who trust him, whoever they are: Rahab welcomed the spies, and she and her family were saved (Joshua 6:22-25; Hebrews 11:31).
The victory belongs to the LORD. He tells Joshua he has already given him the city (6:2).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on how to understand the command to destroy Jericho and its people, and on how this passage relates to the rest of what the Bible says about God's justice and mercy. This page says only what the text says and takes no side.

pages.title: Jonah and the Great Fish
pages.summary: Jonah, a prophet, is sent by the LORD to Nineveh, a great city, to speak out against its wickedness. Jonah sails the other way, boarding a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish, to get away from the LORD. A violent storm rises, the sailors cry out to their gods, and Jonah sleeps below. When the lot falls on Jonah, he tells them to throw him overboard, and when they do, the sea grows calm. A great fish swallows him, and for three days and nights he prays from inside it, until the fish throws him up on dry land. A second time the LORD tells him to go to Nineveh, and this time he does, announcing that in forty days the city will be overturned. Everyone in the city fasts, wears sackcloth and gives up evil ways, and God holds back the disaster. Jonah is angry. God makes a vine grow to shade him, lets it wither, and asks whether he should not care about Nineveh.
pages.look_closer: Notice the reason Jonah gives for running away: he knew God was slow to anger, gracious, and ready to hold back disaster (4:2). The book ends with a question from God (4:11), and does not say how Jonah answered.
lessons: You cannot run from God. Jonah sails the other way, yet God is in the storm, the sea and the great fish (Jonah 1:3-4, 17).
God hears prayer from the deepest trouble. Jonah prays from inside the fish and is brought safely to land (2:1-2, 10).
God gives second chances. He speaks to Jonah again, and this time Jonah goes (3:1-3).

God's mercy reaches even enemies. Nineveh was a city of Assyria, which later conquered Israel (2 Kings 17:5-6). Nineveh turns from evil and God relents (Jonah 3:10), but Jonah is angry, and God asks if he should not care about such a city (4:11).
Jesus points to Jonah as a sign: three days in the great fish, as the Son of Man will spend three days in the earth (Matthew 12:39-41).

context.label: Who Jonah was: a prophet in Israel

pages.title: The Birth of Jesus
pages.summary:
An angel appears to Mary (Luke 1:26-38). Gabriel tells this young woman, engaged to Joseph, that she will bear a son, to be named Jesus and called the Son of the Most High. She asks how this can be, and he answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her. Mary says she is the Lord's servant.

Joseph learns it too (Matthew 1:18-25). Finding Mary expecting, he plans to end the engagement quietly. An angel tells him in a dream that the child is from the Holy Spirit and is to be named Jesus. Joseph does as he is told and takes Mary as his wife.

A census ordered by Caesar Augustus brings them to Bethlehem, where Mary gives birth to her firstborn son and lays him in a manger (Luke 2:1-7). An angel tells nearby shepherds of a Savior, a crowd of angels praises God, and the shepherds hurry to find the baby (2:8-20).
pages.look_closer: Notice how the two accounts fit together. Mary is told to name the child Jesus (Luke 1:31), and Joseph, in a dream, is told the same thing (Matthew 1:21), so both parents hear the name from heaven.
lessons: God keeps his promises. The child to be named Jesus will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), and Matthew says this fulfils what the prophet had spoken (1:22-23).
Mary and Joseph obey God, even when it costs them. Mary says she is the Lord's servant (Luke 1:38), and Joseph does what the angel told him (Matthew 1:24).
God comes humbly. The Saviour is laid in a manger (Luke 2:7), and the first to hear are shepherds (2:8-12).
The news is for everyone: great joy for all the people (Luke 2:10-11). God loved the world so much that he gave his Son (John 3:16).

pages.title: Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
also: the feeding of the five thousand
pages.summary: A large crowd follows Jesus across the Sea of Galilee, drawn by the signs he has been doing for the sick, and the Passover festival is near. When Jesus sees the people coming, he asks Philip where they could buy bread for them all. Philip replies that two hundred denarii could not give each person a small piece. Andrew has found a boy with two little fish and five barley loaves, but wonders what that is among so many. Jesus has everyone sit on the grass, about five thousand men, gives thanks, and shares out the bread and fish until all have as much as they want. He tells his disciples to gather what is left so that nothing is wasted, and they fill twelve baskets. The people say he must be the Prophet who was to come, but Jesus sees that they want to make him king by force, and he withdraws alone to the mountain. He feeds another great crowd later, about four thousand people (Mark 8:1-9).
pages.look_closer: Notice verse 6. Jesus asks Philip a question that he does not need answered, and John tells us why: it was a test, since Jesus already had in mind what he would do. Philip answers with arithmetic, and Andrew with what one boy has with him.
lessons: Jesus does this more than once. Here he feeds about five thousand, and on another occasion about four thousand (Mark 8:1-9; Matthew 15:32-38). He provides for his people again and again.
Jesus uses what we bring. A boy's five loaves and two fish, small as they were, fed the whole crowd (John 6:9-13).

passages.label: The crowd, the question and the boy's food

pages.title: The Good Samaritan
also: the parable of the good Samaritan
pages.summary: An expert in the Law tests Jesus by asking what he must do in order to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks him what the Law says, and he answers that we are to love God completely and our neighbour as ourselves. Wanting to justify himself, the man asks who his neighbour is. Jesus answers with a story. Robbers attack a man on the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho and leave him half dead. A priest and then a Levite see him and move to the opposite side of the road. But a Samaritan is moved with compassion when he sees him. He bandages the wounds with oil and wine, takes the man on his own animal to an inn, looks after him, and leaves money with the innkeeper, promising to repay any extra cost. Jesus asks which of the three was a neighbour; the expert answers that it was the one who showed mercy, and Jesus tells him to go and do the same.
pages.look_closer: Notice how the question is turned around. The man asks who counts as his neighbour (verse 29), but Jesus finishes by asking which of the three acted as a neighbour to the one who was hurt (verse 36).
lessons: Our neighbour is anyone in need, not only people like us. The Samaritan crossed a wall of dislike to help (Luke 10:33, 36-37).
Faith without action is dead. The priest and the Levite knew the Law and passed by (10:31-32; James 2:15-17).
Real love costs something: time, money and effort (10:34-35).
Jesus says: go and do the same (10:37). Mercy is something we do.

passages.label: The story of the man on the road

pages.title: Zacchaeus Meets Jesus
pages.summary: Jesus is passing through Jericho when a wealthy man called Zacchaeus, who is a chief tax collector, tries to see who Jesus is. He is too short to see over the crowd, so he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree along the way Jesus is about to take. When Jesus reaches the spot, he looks up, calls Zacchaeus by name and says he must stay at his house today. Zacchaeus hurries down and welcomes him joyfully, while everyone who sees it complains that Jesus is staying as the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus then stands and tells the Lord he will give half of what he owns to the poor, and that if he has cheated anyone he will pay it back four times over. Jesus says that this house has received salvation today, because Zacchaeus is also a son of Abraham, and that the Son of Man has come to find lost people and save them.
pages.look_closer: Notice the order. Jesus asks to stay at the house (verse 5) before Zacchaeus has said anything about changing, and Zacchaeus makes his promise (verse 8) only after the crowd has begun to grumble.
lessons: Jesus came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10), and he went looking for the man everyone looked down on.
Jesus calls him by name and goes to his house, though the crowd mutters (19:5-7). He is not put off by what others think.
Meeting Jesus changes a life: Zacchaeus gives half of what he owns to the poor and repays four times what he took (19:8), and salvation comes to his house (19:9).
He made an effort to see Jesus: he ran ahead and climbed a tree (19:3-4). God is found by those who look for him with all their heart (Jeremiah 29:13).

pages.title: The Empty Tomb
pages.summary:
On the first day of the week, before dawn, Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb and finds the stone moved (John 20:1). She runs to Peter and the other disciple, and the two run to see. Peter goes in and finds the linen cloths; the other disciple goes in too, and sees and believes (20:2-10).

Mary stays, weeping. She sees two angels, and then a man she takes for the gardener. When he says her name, she knows it is Jesus, alive. He sends her to tell the disciples, and she announces that she has seen the Lord (20:11-18). The other Gospels add that angels told the women he is risen (Matthew 28:5-7; Luke 24:5-6).

Jesus did not leave at once. For forty days he appeared to his followers, showing in many ways that he was alive, to Peter, the Twelve and more than five hundred at once (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:5-6). Then he was taken up into heaven (Acts 1:9).
pages.look_closer: Notice what changes Mary. She has already spoken with Jesus without knowing him (verses 14-15). It is when he says her name that she turns and answers him (verse 16).
lessons: Jesus has risen from the dead. The tomb was empty because he is alive, as he said (Matthew 28:6), and this is the heart of the good news (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
He did not appear only once. For forty days he was on earth, appearing again and again to many people (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:5-8), so that his followers could be sure.

passages.label: Peter and the other disciple run to the tomb
Mary weeps and meets a stranger

pages.title: The Day of Pentecost
also: the Holy Spirit comes at Pentecost
pages.summary: On the day of Pentecost the followers of Jesus are gathered in one room. A sound like a strong wind fills the house, what look like flames settle on every one of them, and all are filled with the Holy Spirit. As the Spirit enables them, they start speaking in other tongues. Devout Jews from many lands are living in Jerusalem, and a crowd gathers, amazed that each one hears God's wonders told in his own language. Some mock and say the believers are drunk. Peter stands up with the Eleven and answers that it is far too early in the day for that. He says that what they see is what the prophet Joel spoke of, and that God has raised the Jesus whom they crucified and made Jesus both Lord and Christ. Deeply moved, the people ask what to do. Peter tells them to repent and be baptized, and promises that they will receive the Holy Spirit as a gift. About three thousand are baptized that day.
pages.look_closer: Notice how wide Peter says the promise reaches: to the people listening, to their children, and to everyone far away whom the Lord will call (verse 39). The words of Joel that he quotes are just as wide: sons and daughters, young and old, even servants (verses 17-18).
lessons: Pentecost was the beginning, not the only time. The Spirit filled the believers in Jerusalem again (Acts 4:31), the Samaritans when Peter and John prayed for them (8:14-17), Cornelius's household (10:44-46) and the disciples at Ephesus (19:1-6).

Peter says the promise is for his listeners, for their children and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord calls (Acts 2:39). Jesus says the Father gives the Holy Spirit to anyone who asks (Luke 11:13).

The same promise is open today to every believer who searches and longs for a closer relationship with God, with Jesus and with the Holy Spirit. The gifts of the Spirit are given for the good of all (1 Corinthians 12:7-11).

passages.label: The Spirit comes and the crowd gathers
Peter speaks, and the people respond

pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on whether being filled with the Holy Spirit, as described here, is a separate experience after new birth or part of coming to faith, and on the place of speaking in tongues today: whether it is a sign of being filled, a gift given to some, or something that belonged to the early church. The summary says only what the passage says; the box "What this teaches us" gives the reading that the promise and the gifts are for believers today.

pages.title: The Woman at the Well
pages.summary: Jesus is heading back to Galilee and has to go through Samaria. He sits down tired by Jacob's well near the town of Sychar while his disciples go to buy food. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus asks her for a drink. She is surprised, since Jews and Samaritans do not mix. Jesus speaks of living water, and she asks for it. He tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she has now is not her husband, and she calls him a prophet. They talk about where people should worship, and Jesus says the Father is looking for those who worship in spirit and in truth. When she says that the Messiah is coming, Jesus tells her that he, the man speaking with her, is that Messiah. She leaves her water jar and hurries into town to tell people to come and see. Many Samaritans believe, ask Jesus to stay, and after two days call him the Savior of the world.
pages.look_closer: Notice how the town comes to believe. The woman's words bring the people out to Jesus (verses 29 and 39), but after two days with him they tell her that now they have heard for themselves (verses 40-42).
lessons: Jesus crosses boundaries: a Jewish teacher asks a Samaritan woman for a drink (John 4:7-9).
Jesus offers living water that satisfies for good (4:10-14). Only he can meet the thirst of the heart.
He knows everything about her and still welcomes her (4:17-19, 29). We cannot hide from God, and we do not need to.
True worship is in spirit and truth, wherever we are (4:23-24). One meeting made her a witness, and a town came to believe (4:28-30, 39-42).

passages.label: A tired traveller asks for a drink

pages.title: The Baptism of Jesus
pages.summary: Crowds have been going out to the Jordan River to be baptized by John the Baptist, confessing their sins, and John has told them that someone far more powerful is coming after him. Now Jesus travels from Galilee to the Jordan and asks John to baptize him. John tries to stop him, saying that he is the one who needs to be baptized by Jesus. Jesus answers that it should happen now, because this is the proper way for them to do everything that is right, and John agrees. As soon as the baptism is over, heaven opens and Jesus sees the Spirit of God come down on him like a dove. A voice from heaven says that this is my Son, the one I love, and I am delighted with him. Luke adds that Jesus was praying at the time.
pages.look_closer: Notice the voice. In Matthew it speaks about Jesus (verse 17), while in Mark and Luke it speaks directly to him (Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22).
lessons: Jesus stands with us. He had no sin, yet he is baptized to do all that is right (Matthew 3:15).
Father, Son and Holy Spirit are all at the Jordan: the Son in the water, the Spirit coming down like a dove, the Father speaking (3:16-17).
The Father speaks his love and approval over Jesus before his ministry begins (3:17; Luke 3:22). We are loved before we have done anything.
The Spirit comes, and then Jesus begins his ministry (Luke 3:21-23; 4:14). Believers, too, are given the Spirit's power to serve (Acts 1:8).

context.label: John the Baptist prepares the way

passages.label: The Spirit and the voice from heaven

pages.title: The Temptation of Jesus
pages.summary: After his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus out into the wilderness, where the devil will tempt him. He fasts for forty days and nights, and he is hungry. The tempter says that if Jesus is God's Son he should order the stones to turn into bread. Jesus replies that bread is not all people live on: they live on every word God speaks. Next the devil takes him to the holy city, sets him on a high point of the temple, and tells him to throw himself down, quoting a promise that angels will lift him up. Jesus replies that Scripture also says not to test the Lord your God. Last, on a high mountain, the devil points out every kingdom of the world and its splendor, and offers them all if Jesus will kneel and worship him. Jesus tells him to go away, for Scripture says the Lord God alone is to be worshiped and served. The devil leaves, and angels come and care for Jesus.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Jesus answers each time from Scripture (verses 4, 7 and 10), and that the devil himself quotes Scripture in the second test (verse 6).
lessons: Jesus answers every temptation with Scripture (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Knowing God's word is our best defence, so read it and learn it.
Be on guard: the devil quotes Scripture too (4:6), but he twists it. We need to know what the whole of Scripture says, as Jesus did (4:7).
Being tempted is not the same as sinning. Jesus was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), so he understands our struggles.
Where Adam and Eve gave way in a garden, Jesus stood firm in the wilderness and obeyed his Father.
Stand up to the devil, and James says he will run away (James 4:7). The devil left Jesus, and angels came and cared for him (Matthew 4:11).

passages.label: On the top of the temple

pages.title: The Parable of the Sower
pages.summary: Beside the lake, a crowd so large gathers that Jesus teaches from a boat while the people stand on the shore. He tells of a farmer scattering seed. Some seed falls on the path, and birds eat it. Some falls on rocky ground and shoots up fast, but the sun scorches it and, with no root, it withers. Some falls among thorns, which choke it. The rest falls on good soil and gives a crop, thirty, sixty or a hundred times over. Alone with the Twelve and others, Jesus is asked about the parable and says the word is what the farmer sows. Some people are like the path: they hear, and Satan takes the word away. Some are like the rocky ground: they receive it gladly but have no root, and fall away when trouble or persecution comes. Some are like the thorns: worries, wealth and other desires choke the word. Others are like the good soil: they hear, receive it and bear a crop.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Jesus says the same thing about every kind of soil: they hear the word (verses 15, 16, 18 and 20). What differs is what happens next.
lessons: The seed is God's word (Mark 4:14). The same word falls on four kinds of heart, and what differs is the soil, not the seed.
The path: the word is heard but not understood, and the enemy takes it away (4:15). Listen closely, and ask when you do not understand, as the disciples asked Jesus (4:10).
Rocky ground: gladness without roots. Faith with no depth falls away when trouble comes (4:16-17). Put down roots in God's word and in prayer.
Thorns: worries, the pull of wealth and wanting more choke the word (4:18-19). Today these crowd every life, so make room for God.
Good soil: hear the word, welcome it and bear fruit, as much as a hundredfold (4:20). Ask yourself which soil you are, and prepare the ground.

pages.title: Jesus Walks on the Water
pages.summary: Jesus sends his disciples ahead in a boat to the far side while he dismisses the crowds. Then he climbs a mountain alone to pray. By evening the boat is far from land, battered by waves and a headwind. Late in the night Jesus comes toward them, walking on the sea. The disciples are terrified and cry out that it is a ghost. At once Jesus tells them to take courage: it is he, and they need not fear. Peter answers that if it is the Lord, he should command him to come on the water. Jesus says come, and Peter climbs out of the boat and walks toward him. But when he notices the wind he is afraid, begins to sink and cries out for the Lord to save him. Jesus reaches out and takes hold of him, asking why he doubted. Once they are in the boat the wind dies down, and the men there worship Jesus, saying he is truly the Son of God.
pages.look_closer: Notice that all three accounts have Jesus saying nearly the same thing to his frightened disciples: that it is he, and that they should not be afraid (Matthew 14:27; Mark 6:50; John 6:20).
lessons: Keep your eyes on Jesus. Peter walks on the water while he looks at Jesus (Matthew 14:29). He starts to sink only when he looks at the wind and the storm instead (14:30).
When you begin to sink, cry out. Peter calls to the Lord to save him, and at once Jesus reaches out and takes hold of him (14:30-31).
Jesus comes to his friends in the middle of the storm, tells them to take heart and says it is he (14:27). He is not far from us in our storms.
Little faith is still faith. Jesus asks why Peter doubted, but he holds on to him, and afterwards they all worship (14:31-33). Fix your eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:2).

pages.title: The Raising of Lazarus
pages.summary: Lazarus of Bethany is sick, so his sisters Martha and Mary send word to Jesus, who loves all three. Jesus says the sickness is for God's glory, yet stays where he is two more days. Then he tells his disciples they will go back to Judea, and says plainly that Lazarus has died. When he arrives, Lazarus has lain in the tomb for four days. Martha meets him and says that if he had been there her brother would not have died. Jesus tells her that he is the resurrection and the life, and she answers that she believes he is the Christ, the Son of God. Mary later says the same to him. Seeing the weeping, Jesus is deeply moved and weeps. At the tomb, a cave closed with a stone, he has the stone removed, thanks the Father and calls for Lazarus to come out. The dead man comes out, still wrapped in linen, and Jesus tells them to take off the cloths and let him go.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Jesus weeps (verse 35), though he has already told his disciples he is going to wake Lazarus (verse 11). The onlookers are divided: some see how much he loved him, and others ask why he did not prevent the death (verses 36-37).
lessons: Jesus says he is the resurrection and the life, and that anyone who trusts him will live, even if he dies (John 11:25-26).
Jesus weeps (11:35). He is not far from our grief: he feels it with us.
A delay is not a denial. Jesus waited two days so that God would be glorified (11:4-6, 40).
Jesus calls Lazarus by name and the dead man comes out (11:43-44): a sign of Jesus' own resurrection, and of the day when the dead will hear his voice (5:28-29).

passages.label: Word comes that Lazarus is sick

pages.title: The Road to Emmaus
pages.summary: On the first day of the week, two of Jesus' followers are walking to Emmaus, a village seven miles away from Jerusalem. Jesus himself joins them, but something keeps them from recognizing him. He asks what they are discussing, and they stop, looking sad. Cleopas asks whether he alone has not heard of recent events. They tell of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified after the chief priests and rulers handed him over, and say they had hoped he would redeem Israel. Some women, they add, did not find his body and spoke of angels who said he lives. Jesus says they are slow to believe the prophets and, starting with Moses, explains what all the Scriptures say about him. At the village they urge him to stay. At the table he takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and their eyes are opened; he vanishes. They hurry back to Jerusalem, where the Eleven and their companions are saying the Lord has risen, and the two tell what happened.
pages.look_closer: Notice when they recognize him. Afterward they say their hearts were burning as he opened the Scriptures to them (verse 32), but their eyes are opened as he breaks the bread (verses 30-31 and 35).
lessons: Jesus walks beside us even when we do not recognise him (Luke 24:15-16).
The Scriptures point to Christ: beginning with Moses and every prophet, Jesus showed them what the Scriptures say about himself (24:27). Their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures (24:32).
He is known in the breaking of bread (24:30-31, 35). Jesus is found where his people gather and share.
Good news is meant to be shared: they went back to Jerusalem that same hour to tell the others (24:33-35).

passages.label: A stranger joins two sad travellers

pages.title: Nicodemus Visits Jesus
pages.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a Jewish leader, comes to Jesus at night. He says Jesus must be a teacher from God, since nobody could do such signs unless God were with him. Jesus tells him that unless a person is born again he cannot see God's kingdom. Nicodemus asks how an old man can be born, and whether he can go back into his mother's womb to be born. Jesus says that no one enters God's kingdom without being born of water and the Spirit, and compares everyone born of the Spirit to the wind. Nicodemus asks how this can be. Jesus asks how Israel's teacher can fail to understand, and says that, as Moses raised the snake in the wilderness, the Son of Man has to be lifted up, so that all who believe in him will have eternal life. The passage goes on to say that God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son, to save it, not to condemn it.
pages.look_closer: Notice how Nicodemus understands the words. He asks whether an old man can go back into his mother's womb to be born (verse 4), and Jesus replies by speaking of water, the Spirit and the wind (verses 5-8).
lessons: Jesus speaks of a change of heart. God promised long before to write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33) and to give a new heart and put his Spirit within us (Ezekiel 36:26-27): not on tablets of stone but on human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3).
What renews us is a relationship with God and with Jesus, which begins by believing in him (John 3:16). Baptism is then the natural next step for someone who has chosen to follow him (Matthew 28:19).
Look at Jesus' own baptism. When John baptized him in the Jordan, the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove (Matthew 3:16). It helps us see what being born of the Spirit means.
pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on what it means to be born again, or born of water and the Spirit: whether the water points to baptism, to natural birth or to cleansing, and how new birth relates to baptism, to faith, and to the baptism in the Holy Spirit. The summary says only what the passage says; the box "What this teaches us" gives the reading that this is a change of heart, with baptism as the natural next step.

pages.title: Adam and Eve in the Garden
pages.summary: The LORD God makes a man from the dust and breathes life into him. In a garden in Eden he sets the tree of life and a tree that gives knowledge of good and evil, and warns that eating from the second means death. He makes a woman from one of the man's ribs, as a partner for him. A crafty serpent tells the woman she will not die, and she eats the fruit and gives some to her husband. They realize they are naked and hide. Asked what happened, the man blames the woman, who blames the serpent. God speaks to each of them: pain and hard work, and in the end death, for the man will return to the dust. Even so, God makes garments of skin and clothes them himself. Then he sends them out of Eden, away from the tree of life.
pages.look_closer: Notice that God speaks to them before he passes sentence. He asks questions (verses 9-13), and before they leave the garden he makes clothes of skin and dresses them himself (verse 21).
lessons: Disobedience brought sin into the world, and with it death, just as God had warned (Genesis 2:17; 3:19). Paul sums it up: the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23).

God did not leave them uncovered. He made garments of skins and clothed them himself (Genesis 3:21), the first covering for their shame, and it cost an animal its life. Later God says that life is in the blood, given on the altar to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11).

The rest of the Bible unfolds to answer this first failure. Where sin means death, God allowed a substitute: an innocent animal, often a lamb, took the sinner's place. Isaiah pictures a coming substitute, led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7).
Ultimately Jesus became the final lamb, who died for our salvation to pay for sin all the way back to Adam and Eve. Our disobedience to God has serious consequences, as this story shows.

passages.label: The man, the garden and the woman
The serpent, the fruit and leaving Eden

pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on how to read these chapters (literally, as history told in figures, or as a story that teaches), on what the fall means for people, including the doctrine of original sin, and on how far the garments of skin and the later sacrifices point forward to Christ. The summary says only what the text says; the box "What this teaches us" gives the reading that links these events to Christ.

pages.title: The Call of Abraham
pages.summary: The LORD tells Abram, whom God will later rename Abraham, to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house and go to a land that God will show him. God promises to make him a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to bless every family on earth through him. Abram goes, aged seventy-five, bringing his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, with everything they own into Canaan. There the LORD appears and says he will give this land to Abram's offspring, and Abram builds an altar. He moves on, builds another altar near Bethel, and calls on the LORD's name. Later, in a vision, God tells Abram not to be afraid, for he is his shield. Abram answers that he has no child, so a servant will inherit. God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars if he can, for his offspring will be as many. Abram believes the LORD, who counts it to him as righteousness.
pages.look_closer: Notice how large the promises are beside Abram's situation. He has no child (15:2-3), yet God promises a great nation and a blessing for every family on earth (12:2-3), and offspring like the stars (15:5).
lessons: God calls Abram out of a comfortable life: a settled home with his family and his possessions (Genesis 12:1, 5; 13:2). He is sent to a land he does not know, and he listens and goes (12:4; Hebrews 11:8).
God makes a promise and keeps it, even though it takes years. Abram is seventy-five when he is called (Genesis 12:4) and a hundred when Isaac is born (21:5).
Abram believes the LORD, who counts it to him as righteousness (15:6; Romans 4:3). Faith, not comfort, is what God looks for.
God walks with him. He says to Abram to walk before him and be blameless (17:1).
When the promised son has been born, God tests him again, and Abraham stands fast, walking with God and trusting him (22:1-3; Hebrews 11:17-19).

pages.title: Abraham and Isaac
pages.summary:
God tests Abraham (Genesis 22:1). He tells him to take Isaac, the son he waited so long for, his only son, whom he loves, and offer him as a burnt offering on a mountain in Moriah (22:2).

Abraham obeys. He rises early and sets out with Isaac, two servants and the wood (22:3). On the third day he sees the place and leaves the servants behind (22:4-5). Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham answers that God himself will provide it (22:6-8).

At the place Abraham builds an altar, ties Isaac up and lifts the knife (22:9-10). The angel of the LORD calls from heaven and stops him (22:11-12). Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns and offers it in place of his son. He names the place The LORD Will Provide (22:13-14).

The angel speaks again: God promises to bless all nations through Abraham's offspring (22:15-18).
pages.look_closer: Notice how God names the son one step at a time: his son, his only son, the one he loves, and only then Isaac (22:2). Notice too Abraham's answer on the way up: God will provide the lamb (22:8).
lessons: The wood and the lamb. Isaac carries the wood (22:6) and asks where the lamb is. Abraham answers that God himself will provide it (22:8), more truly than he knew.
The ram. It is caught by its horns and dies in Isaac's place (22:13): an innocent substitute, so that the child could live. Israel's altars kept this picture before the people until its fulfilment.
The blueprint for Jesus. Another beloved, only Son carried the wood of his own sacrifice (John 19:17), near the same Jerusalem ridge (2 Chronicles 3:1), and is called the Lamb of God (John 1:29).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians differ on how to understand God testing Abraham with this command, and on how far the account is meant to match the cross. Many see Isaac, the ram and the wood as a picture pointing to Jesus. The summary says only what the text says; the box "What this teaches us" gives that reading.

pages.title: Joseph and His Brothers
pages.summary: Joseph is the son his father Jacob loves most, and his brothers hate him, all the more after dreams that seem to say they will bow down to him. When he finds them at Dothan, they plot to kill him. Reuben says not to, and to use an empty pit instead, and Judah suggests selling him, so he is sold to traders heading for Egypt. The brothers show Jacob a robe stained with goat's blood, and he mourns, believing a wild animal has killed his son. In Egypt Joseph serves Potiphar, and the LORD stays with him, but when he refuses Potiphar's wife she lies about him, and he is thrown into prison, where the LORD stays with him again. Later he explains Pharaoh's dreams, crediting God: seven good years, then seven of famine. Pharaoh puts him over all Egypt. At last Joseph reveals who he is to his brothers, weeping, and tells them not to blame themselves, because God sent him ahead to save lives.
pages.look_closer: Notice that Joseph does not pretend nothing happened. He says plainly that they sold him (verse 4), and then says that God sent him ahead to save lives (verses 5 and 7).
lessons: God's plan is greater than ours, even when we do not understand it. Joseph says that God sent him ahead to save lives (Genesis 45:5-7), and that what his brothers meant for evil, God meant for good (50:20).
God is with us in hardship. In Potiphar's house and in prison the LORD was with Joseph (39:2-3, 21-23). The pit, the slave market and the cell were not the end of the story (Psalms 105:17-19).
God uses trials to prepare us and to make us a pillar for others. From prison Joseph is raised up to save Egypt and his own family (41:39-41, 57).
Joseph gives God the credit for his gift (41:16). He forgives his brothers, weeps over them and speaks kindly to them (45:1-15; 50:19-21): hardship has not made him bitter.

passages.label: The dreams, the pit and the sale
Joseph tells his brothers who he is

pages.title: The Burning Bush
also: the bush that did not burn up
pages.summary: Moses, who fled Egypt as a young man, is shepherding for his father-in-law, Jethro, when he reaches Horeb, the mountain of God. The angel of the LORD appears to him as a flame inside a bush that burns but is not used up. As Moses goes closer to look, God calls his name from the bush, telling him to stay back and take off his sandals, because the ground is holy. God says he is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses hides his face. God has seen his people's suffering in Egypt and heard their cries, and has come down to free them. He is sending Moses to Pharaoh. When Moses asks who he is to go, God promises to be with him. Asked what name to give the Israelites, God says I AM WHO I AM, the LORD, the God of their ancestors. He warns that Pharaoh will not let them go until wonders strike Egypt.
pages.look_closer: Notice how God answers the question "Who am I?" (verse 11). He does not tell Moses who he is. He promises to be with him, and gives a sign that comes only after the task is done: worship on this mountain (verse 12).
lessons: God chooses the unlikely. Moses says he has never been eloquent and is slow of speech and tongue, which many understand as a stammer, and God answers that he made the mouth and will help him speak (Exodus 4:10-12).
God does not wait until we feel ready. Moses asks who he is to go, and God does not praise his strengths but promises to be with him (3:11-12).

Expect resistance. God tells Moses from the start that the king will not let the people go the first time he asks, but only after mighty wonders (3:19-20). Obeying God does not promise an easy welcome, and his plan still stands.
God sees, hears and comes down. He has seen his people's suffering and heard their cry (3:7-8). He knows what you are going through.
God is holy. Moses is told to take off his sandals, because the ground is holy (3:5): we come to God with reverence.

context.label: Before the bush: Moses flees Egypt and becomes a shepherd

passages.label: God calls Moses from the bush

pages.title: Ruth and Naomi
pages.summary: In the days of the judges a famine drives Elimelech, his wife Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem to Moab. Elimelech dies, the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and then both sons die too. When Naomi hears that the LORD has given his people food, she heads home and urges her daughters-in-law to go back to their families. Orpah turns back, but Ruth clings to Naomi and promises to go where she goes, to take Naomi's people and God as her own, and to stay until death. In Bethlehem Naomi says she has come home empty. Ruth gleans barley in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's husband, and he treats her kindly. At Naomi's urging, Ruth goes at night to Boaz on the threshing floor and asks him to act as her family's redeemer. At the town gate a nearer relative gives up his right, and Boaz buys back the family's land and marries Ruth. Their son Obed becomes the grandfather of David.
pages.look_closer: Notice how the book keeps pointing to where Ruth comes from. She is called a Moabite again and again (for example 1:22, 2:2 and 4:10), and yet the story ends with her great-grandson, David (4:17-22).
lessons: No matter who you are or where you come from, God chooses you and has a plan for you. Ruth is a Moabite, a foreigner (Ruth 1:4; 2:10), yet she becomes the great-grandmother of King David (4:13-17) and has a place in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
You are valuable, important and loved. Boaz calls Ruth a woman of noble character (Ruth 3:11), and God says of his people that they are precious and honored in his sight, and loved (Isaiah 43:4).
Faithfulness is not forgotten. Ruth stays with Naomi and chooses Naomi's God (1:16-17), and God provides for them both through Boaz, who redeems them (4:9-10).
God works through ordinary days. Ruth goes out to glean and happens to come to the field of Boaz (2:3): what looks like chance is part of God's plan.

passages.label: Naomi and Ruth come to Bethlehem
Ruth and Boaz at the threshing floor
Boaz redeems, and Obed is born

pages.title: Samuel Hears God
pages.summary: The boy Samuel serves the LORD alongside Eli, in days when messages from God are rare. One night, as Samuel lies down near the ark of God in the LORD's house, the LORD calls to him. He runs to Eli, but Eli did not call and sends him back to bed. It happens a second time, and a third, for Samuel does not yet know the LORD. Then Eli realizes who is calling and tells Samuel how to answer if it happens again. The LORD comes and stands there, calling Samuel's name twice, and Samuel answers that he is listening. God tells him he is about to act against Eli's family, because Eli's sons did wrong against God and Eli did not stop them. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell Eli, but Eli presses him, and Samuel hides nothing. Eli says the LORD must do what he sees as good. Samuel grows, the LORD is with him, and all Israel knows he is a prophet.
pages.look_closer: Notice the pattern. Samuel goes to Eli three times (verses 5, 6 and 8) before Eli realizes who is calling, and only after that does the LORD come and stand there (verse 10).
lessons: Hearing the calling is not yet hearing the message. Three times Samuel hears his name and thinks it is Eli (1 Samuel 3:4-8). He hears only the calling.
The message comes when Samuel says he is listening. Only then does the LORD give him the word (3:9-11). God is revealed when we listen, not when we speak: when we are tuned to his voice.
Scripture says the same. Be quick to listen and slow to speak (James 1:19). Be still and know that God is God (Psalms 46:10). Jesus says his sheep listen to his voice (John 10:27).
We can be helped to hear. It is Eli who tells Samuel how to answer (3:9): sometimes God uses the older and wiser to show us how to listen.
